extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, regulators, and policymakers (those interested in rulemaking design and notice-and-comment procedures)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical framework for evaluating the costs and benefits of procedural 'ossification' in notice-and-comment rulemaking, including when delay and resource-intensive procedures can be beneficial (commitment, legitimacy) and when speed or exceptions are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer less resource-intensive procedures when quality equal
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a regulatory process could create equally nonarbitrary and scientifically sound regulations without requiring as many agency resources, then it too should be preferred.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a baseline efficiency preference: when two procedures produce rules of equal quality (nonarbitrary, scientifically sound), choose the one that requires fewer agency resources and less delay. The passage frames this as a default normative rule (who could be in favor of waste?). Use this criterion when comparing procedural designs that yield similar substantive outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept tradeoffs of some quality for speed/cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: “Even if it is not possible to create delay-free procedures that generate equally high-quality rules, it still may be desirable to surrender some quality for increased speed and cost savings.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a legitimate tradeoff: faster, cheaper procedures that slightly reduce rule quality can be preferable in some contexts. Apply when timeliness or resource constraints create greater social value than marginal gains in decision accuracy. Consider opportunity costs of delay described in the text when weighing this tradeoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossification increases the cost and difficulty of regulatory change
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ossification makes change more difficult; because of administrative law’s procedures, it takes agencies more time and effort to change the regulatory environment than would be the case absent those procedures.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat procedural requirements as real costs that slow or divert agency resources. Use this criterion to predict that more burdensome procedures will reduce the frequency and speed of regulatory change; evaluate procedural proposals by their marginal effect on the cost of changing rules. The text notes that even if some claims about burdens are overstated, procedures impose at least some delay by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory durability increases regulated parties' confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is more difficult for agencies to make regulatory change, regulated parties can have relatively greater confidence that regulations that now exist will continue to exist than would be reasonable to expect in an ossification-free world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative benefit of procedures: predict that more durable rules reduce uncertainty for regulated parties. The paper explains how external enforcement (courts, OIRA) strengthens this durability and thus party expectations. Apply in cost–benefit assessments that value private-sector reliance and long-term planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability encourages private investment via lower discounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Because regulated parties can expect incentives to persist, they use a smaller 'discount factor' in cost–benefit calculations and are more likely to make capital-intensive investments (example: costly plant to obtain agency incentive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether to retain or add procedural hurdles, consider whether the resulting increased certainty will mobilize private investment that agencies otherwise could not solicit. The paper gives a stylized numerical example (10,000,000 plant cost vs. 1,000,000/year incentive). Consider how much smaller incentives the agency could offer if durability lowers private-sector discounting. This is a concrete mechanism by which ossification can expand an agency's regulatory toolkit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossification can expand an agency’s menu of feasible regulatory options
rubrics_metrics.description: Ossification sometimes may expand rather than contract an agency's regulatory menu, especially for long-run objectives that require substantial private investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate procedural design not only by its restraining effects but also by whether it enables commitments and incentives that the agency could not credibly offer in a low-ossification world. Use this criterion when agencies aim to induce long-term private behavior (e.g., innovation, infrastructure) through regulatory incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: External enforcement (courts/OIRA) makes procedural commitments credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Durability of schemes is enhanced because external actors like courts or OIRA often enforce regulatory procedures; the agency cannot simply change procedures without compliance or review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the credibility of commitments created by procedure, account for enforcement by judicial review and executive oversight (OIRA). The EPA methane example and Clean Air Council litigation illustrate how courts/OIRA can prevent rapid reversals and thus concretely support the commitment function of ossification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossification not valuable when agency needs immediate action (emerging risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are situations in which ossification is not especially valuable because the agency does not need a credible commitment mechanism to encourage private-sector behavior; for example, when the agency must act immediately to stop an emerging practice it believes is dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this negative/limiting criterion: weigh the social costs of delay in contexts of urgent harm (public health, imminent environmental risk). Consider statutory 'good cause' exceptions (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(3)(B)) that allow agencies to bypass notice-and-comment when procedures are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest. Use in emergency-response evaluations and when timeliness dominates the value of commitment or legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay allows information intermediaries to function and can enhance legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: By giving 'information intermediaries' time to act, members of the public have more opportunities to learn what is afoot; delayed agency decisions increase the chance that nonspecialists will understand proposals, which enhances agency legitimacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative criterion focused on democratic legitimacy: procedures that slow decisionmaking enable media, civil society, and social networks to surface information, critique, and context. The text argues that this process can increase public trust and acceptance of agency action; but also cautions intermediaries are imperfect and false claims can spread. Consider the tradeoff between speed and the societal value of public comprehension and participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public understanding fostered by delay strengthens cooperative compliance and political support
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of trust creates legitimacy problems; delay provides more time for nonspecialists to understand agency action and to express agreement or disagreement, increasing the public's willingness to cooperate or approve expanded agency missions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating procedures, include long-run political economy effects: whether delay improves the perceived fairness and acceptability of agency actions, thereby making enforcement and future delegations easier. The passage links this to constitutional design (slow lawmaking via bicameralism-and-presentment) as a parallel reason to accept procedural delay for important regulatory changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ossification disproportionately affects significant regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Richard Pierce's contention that ossification only affects the most significant regulations; these are the regulations for which public awareness and time for deliberation are most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the legitimacy and commitment benefits of procedural friction for high-stakes/major rules. In cost–benefit or design choices, treat 'significance' as a moderator: procedural burdens that produce delay may be most defensible for major rules, less so for minor ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical signal: administrations race to finalize rules before leaving office
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrations often race to finish rules before they leave power because finished rules have staying power and the next administration cannot simply eliminate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical/political behavior as an indicator of the perceived effectiveness of procedures: agencies and administrations exploit the durability benefit of final rules. When designing or evaluating procedural reforms, anticipate strategic timing behavior and its implications for regulatory stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause exception allows bypassing notice-and-comment in special circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the APA requirements do not apply 'when the agency for good cause finds ... that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.' (5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(3)(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering whether to apply full notice-and-comment, explicitly assess whether facts justify invoking the good-cause exception (e.g., urgent danger, impracticability). This is a statutory constraint that functions as a built-in, context-specific override of ossification; weigh its use carefully because bypassing procedures sacrifices the commitment and legitimacy benefits described above.
